cards.front: What is the primary purpose of cost accounting?
cards.back: To determine the cost of products, services, or activities for decision-making and control purposes

cards.front: What is the difference between cost accounting and financial accounting?
cards.back: Cost accounting focuses on internal decision-making and cost control, while financial accounting focuses on external reporting

cards.front: What are the three main elements of cost?
cards.back: Direct materials, direct labor, and manufacturing overhead

cards.front: What is the difference between direct and indirect costs?
cards.back: Direct costs can be traced to specific products, while indirect costs cannot be directly traced

cards.front: What is the formula for calculating total manufacturing cost?
cards.back: Total Manufacturing Cost = Direct Materials + Direct Labor + Manufacturing Overhead

cards.front: What is the difference between fixed and variable costs?
cards.back: Fixed costs remain constant regardless of production volume, while variable costs change with production volume

cards.front: What is the purpose of cost allocation?
cards.back: To assign indirect costs to cost objects (products, services, or departments) using appropriate allocation bases

cards.front: What is the difference between job costing and process costing?
cards.back: Job costing is used for unique products, while process costing is used for identical products produced continuously

cards.front: What is the formula for calculating predetermined overhead rate?
cards.back: Predetermined Overhead Rate = Estimated Total Overhead / Estimated Total Allocation Base

cards.front: What is the difference between actual and normal costing?
cards.back: Actual costing uses actual overhead rates, while normal costing uses predetermined overhead rates

cards.front: What is the purpose of cost-volume-profit (CVP) analysis?
cards.back: To analyze the relationship between costs, volume, and profit to make business decisions

cards.front: What is the formula for calculating contribution margin?
cards.back: Contribution Margin = Sales Revenue - Variable Costs

cards.front: What is the difference between absorption and variable costing?
cards.back: Absorption costing includes all manufacturing costs, while variable costing includes only variable manufacturing costs

cards.front: What is the purpose of standard costing?
cards.back: To establish predetermined costs for comparison with actual costs and identify variances

cards.front: What is the formula for calculating break-even point in units?
cards.back: Break-even Point (Units) = Fixed Costs / (Selling Price per Unit - Variable Cost per Unit)

cards.front: What is the difference between relevant and irrelevant costs?
cards.back: Relevant costs affect decision-making, while irrelevant costs do not affect the decision

cards.front: What is the purpose of activity-based costing (ABC)?
cards.back: To allocate overhead costs based on activities that drive costs, providing more accurate product costs

cards.front: What is the formula for calculating cost of goods manufactured?
cards.back: Cost of Goods Manufactured = Beginning WIP + Total Manufacturing Costs - Ending WIP

cards.front: What is the difference between prime costs and conversion costs?
cards.back: Prime costs include direct materials and direct labor, while conversion costs include direct labor and overhead

cards.front: What is the purpose of variance analysis?
cards.back: To identify and analyze differences between actual and standard costs for control purposes

cards.front: What is the formula for calculating margin of safety?
cards.back: Margin of Safety = Actual Sales - Break-even Sales

cards.front: What is the difference between sunk costs and opportunity costs?
cards.back: Sunk costs are past costs that cannot be recovered, while opportunity costs are benefits foregone from alternatives

cards.front: What is the purpose of cost behavior analysis?
cards.back: To understand how costs change with changes in activity levels for planning and decision-making

cards.front: What is the formula for calculating degree of operating leverage?
cards.back: Degree of Operating Leverage = Contribution Margin / Net Operating Income

cards.front: What is the difference between controllable and uncontrollable costs?
cards.back: Controllable costs can be influenced by management decisions, while uncontrollable costs cannot

cards.front: What is the purpose of cost centers?
cards.back: To accumulate costs for specific departments or activities for control and performance measurement

cards.front: What is the formula for calculating target profit in units?
cards.back: Target Profit (Units) = (Fixed Costs + Target Profit) / (Selling Price per Unit - Variable Cost per Unit)

cards.front: What is the difference between incremental and differential costs?
cards.back: Incremental costs are additional costs from an alternative, while differential costs are the difference between alternatives

cards.front: What is the purpose of responsibility accounting?
cards.back: To assign costs and revenues to specific managers for performance evaluation and control

cards.front: What is the formula for calculating cost per equivalent unit?
cards.back: Cost per Equivalent Unit = Total Costs / Total Equivalent Units

cards.front: What is the difference between joint costs and separable costs?
cards.back: Joint costs are incurred before split-off point, while separable costs are incurred after split-off point

cards.front: What is the purpose of cost estimation?
cards.back: To predict future costs for budgeting, planning, and decision-making purposes

cards.front: What is the formula for calculating overhead variance?
cards.back: Overhead Variance = Actual Overhead - Applied Overhead

cards.front: What is the difference between avoidable and unavoidable costs?
cards.back: Avoidable costs can be eliminated by discontinuing an activity, while unavoidable costs cannot

cards.front: What is the purpose of cost control?
cards.back: To monitor and manage costs to ensure they stay within budget and achieve profitability targets

cards.front: What is the formula for calculating cost of goods sold?
cards.back: Cost of Goods Sold = Beginning Inventory + Cost of Goods Manufactured - Ending Inventory

cards.front: What is the difference between committed and discretionary costs?
cards.back: Committed costs are long-term obligations, while discretionary costs can be adjusted in the short term

cards.front: What is the purpose of cost reporting?
cards.back: To provide management with cost information for decision-making, control, and performance evaluation

cards.front: What is the formula for calculating contribution margin ratio?
cards.back: Contribution Margin Ratio = Contribution Margin / Sales Revenue

cards.front: What is the difference between product costs and period costs?
cards.back: Product costs are inventoried until sold, while period costs are expensed in the period incurred

cards.front: What is the purpose of cost management?
cards.back: To plan, control, and optimize costs to achieve organizational objectives and competitive advantage

cards.front: What is the formula for calculating return on investment (ROI)?
cards.back: ROI = Net Operating Income / Average Operating Assets

cards.front: What is the difference between direct and indirect materials?
cards.back: Direct materials become part of the product, while indirect materials support production but don't become part of the product

cards.front: What is the purpose of cost accounting standards?
cards.back: To ensure consistency, comparability, and reliability in cost accounting practices and reporting

cards.front: What is the formula for calculating residual income?
cards.back: Residual Income = Net Operating Income - (Required Rate of Return × Average Operating Assets)

cards.front: What is the difference between direct and indirect labor?
cards.back: Direct labor works directly on products, while indirect labor supports production but doesn't work directly on products

cards.front: What is the purpose of cost accounting systems?
cards.back: To collect, process, and report cost information for management decision-making and control

cards.front: What is the formula for calculating economic value added (EVA)?
cards.back: EVA = Net Operating Income - (Cost of Capital × Average Operating Assets)

cards.front: What is the difference between manufacturing and non-manufacturing costs?
cards.back: Manufacturing costs are product costs, while non-manufacturing costs are period costs

cards.front: What is the purpose of cost accounting information?
cards.back: To support planning, control, decision-making, and performance evaluation in organizations

cards.front: What is the formula for calculating throughput?
cards.back: Throughput = Sales Revenue - Direct Materials Cost

cards.front: What is the difference between cost accounting and management accounting?
cards.back: Cost accounting focuses on cost determination, while management accounting provides broader information for management

cards.front: What is the purpose of cost accounting principles?
cards.back: To provide guidelines for consistent and reliable cost measurement, allocation, and reporting
